opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the starting point is to look at what's happened to the hardware landscape. For decades we got performance improvements essentially for free from Moore's Law and Dennard scaling, and general-purpose processors just kept getting faster. That's over. Dennard scaling ended in the mid-2000s, and Moore's Law has slowed considerably. So if you want continued improvements in performance and energy efficiency, you have to get them from specialization: building architectures matched to the computation you care about.

At the same time, machine learning has become the dominant workload. What's interesting about ML from an architect's point of view is that these models are naturally expressed as dataflow graphs. You have operators, tensors flowing between them, and a lot of parallelism at multiple levels. Yet we've traditionally executed them on instruction-based machines, CPUs and GPUs, where you fetch and decode instructions and move data back and forth to memory between kernels. That wastes a lot of energy and bandwidth on overhead that isn't really the computation.

The idea behind reconfigurable dataflow is: why not configure the hardware to look like the dataflow graph itself? You lay out the computation spatially across compute and memory units, and data streams from one operator to the next on-chip, without round trips to off-chip memory. You get the efficiency of specialization while staying programmable, because you can reconfigure the chip for a different model or a different part of the model.

The "dynamic" part matters because ML keeps evolving. Early on, models were fairly regular, dense matrix multiplies and convolutions. Now we have sparsity, mixture-of-experts, dynamic shapes, data-dependent control flow, and inference with very different characteristics from training. If your architecture is only good at static, regular computation, you'll be left behind as the algorithms change. So we've been asking how to build dataflow architectures that handle irregularity and data-dependent behavior efficiently and can reconfigure quickly as the workload shifts.

The other piece I've always cared about is the software. Hardware alone doesn't win. You need high-level programming abstractions and compilers that take a model written in something like PyTorch and map it efficiently onto the hardware. A lot of our research, going back to the domain-specific language work at Stanford, has been about that co-design between programming models, compilers, and architecture. Reconfigurable dataflow is a natural target for that approach, because the dataflow abstraction in the software lines up so well with the hardware.

So for me it brings together several threads: the end of easy scaling, the rise of ML as the key workload, and the need for systems that are both efficient and flexible enough to keep up with how fast the algorithms change.

r001.rationale: It says ML workloads are changing and increasingly include sparsity, mixture-of-experts, dynamic shapes, and data-dependent behavior, motivating architectures that adapt as workloads shift.

r002.rationale: It mentions reconfiguring the chip for a different model or part of a model, but does not say to reconfigure only a portion of the dataflow system to execute a different computation graph.

r003.rationale: It does not compare dynamic dataflow architectures with the shift from static VLIW scheduling to runtime CPU scheduling.

r004.rationale: It describes efficient handling of irregularity and flexibility, but does not state that adding dynamism must preserve the architecture’s existing advantages.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the starting point for me is that if you look at where the gains in performance and energy efficiency are going to come from over the next decade, they're not going to come from transistor scaling the way they used to. Moore's Law has slowed dramatically, Dennard scaling ended a long time ago, and so the only lever we really have left is specialization: matching the architecture much more closely to the computation you actually want to run.

Now, the obvious way to specialize is to build a fixed-function ASIC. And that works beautifully as long as the workload doesn't change. The problem with AI is that the workloads change constantly. If you had built a chip around the models that were hot five or six years ago, you'd have something tuned for convolutional networks, and then transformers came along and completely changed the compute and memory access patterns. Now we're seeing mixture-of-experts, sparsity, very long context, agentic workloads where the shape of the computation varies from request to request. The algorithms are moving faster than a hardware design cycle, which is two or three years at minimum. So a purely fixed design is a bad bet.

On the other side you have GPUs, which are very general and very programmable, but they pay for that generality. The instruction-fetch, decode, register-file traffic, the whole von Neumann control structure costs you a lot of energy per operation, and you spend a tremendous amount of effort moving data in and out of memory hierarchies that weren't really designed for these access patterns.

What attracted me to reconfigurable dataflow is that it sits in a sweet spot between those two. The idea is that you take the computation, which in machine learning is naturally expressed as a dataflow graph, and you map that graph spatially onto the chip. You have arrays of compute units and memory units connected by a programmable interconnect, and you configure them so that data flows directly from one operation to the next without going back to a central memory. You've essentially built a custom pipeline for that particular model. You get the efficiency that looks a lot like an ASIC, because you've eliminated most of the overhead of instruction processing and you've kept data on-chip and local.

And the "dynamic" part matters because you don't want to pay a reconfiguration cost every time something changes, and you don't want to be stuck with a single static mapping. Real models have phases: attention looks different from the feed-forward layers, decode looks different from prefill, and in things like mixture-of-experts the routing is data-dependent. So you want hardware that can reconfigure quickly, on the timescale of the computation, and a compiler stack that can reason about that. That's actually where a lot of the interesting research is for us at Stanford: it's as much about the software, the intermediate representations, the mapping and scheduling problem, as it is about the silicon.

So to summarize, I see it as the most practical way to get specialization-level efficiency while keeping up with a field where the algorithms refuse to sit still. And given how much energy AI is consuming now, I think that efficiency isn't a nice-to-have anymore; it's going to determine what's economically and environmentally feasible to build.

r001.rationale: It says AI workloads change constantly and algorithms move faster than hardware design cycles, motivating hardware that can reconfigure quickly.

r002.rationale: It discusses reconfiguring hardware for changing phases and computations, but does not say to reconfigure only a portion of the dataflow system.

r003.rationale: It does not compare dynamic dataflow architectures to the shift from static VLIW scheduling to runtime CPU scheduling.

r004.rationale: It presents dynamic reconfiguration as a way to keep pace with changing workloads while retaining specialization-level efficiency, an existing advantage of dataflow architectures.

astra-6.text:
Well, the fundamental issue is that AI demands an enormous amount of computation, but doing that computation efficiently is often about how you move the data. If you’re constantly moving data back and forth between memory and the compute units, you’re spending time and energy on movement rather than useful work.

With a reconfigurable dataflow architecture, the idea is to organize the hardware around the computation. You map operations onto compute resources and establish the paths that data takes between them. That lets you keep data close to where it’s being used and exploit parallelism across the computation.

The reconfigurability is important because AI workloads keep changing. You want the efficiency of hardware that’s tailored to a particular computation, but you also want the flexibility to support a different model or a different set of operations. For me, that makes this a compelling research direction: how do we bring together the architecture and the software so that programmers can get that efficiency without having to design hardware themselves?

r001.rationale: It says AI workloads keep changing and motivates reconfigurability as a way to support different models or operations.

r002.rationale: It does not propose reconfiguring only part of a dataflow system to run a different computation graph.

r003.rationale: It makes no analogy to the shift from static VLIW scheduling to runtime CPU scheduling.

r004.rationale: It says reconfigurability should provide flexibility while retaining the efficiency of hardware tailored to a computation.

sol-6.1.text:
The central idea is that we need to rethink how computation moves through a machine. In a conventional processor, you spend a lot of energy moving data between memory and the units doing the computation, and issuing instructions to tell those units what to do. For AI workloads, that overhead can be substantial.

With a reconfigurable dataflow architecture, you configure the hardware around the computation. You map operations onto compute resources and arrange for data to flow directly between them. That gives you opportunities to exploit parallelism, keep data close to where it’s used, and avoid unnecessary memory traffic.

The reconfigurability is important because AI algorithms keep changing. You want the efficiency of hardware tailored to a particular computation, but you also want the flexibility to support a new model or a different mix of operations. For me, that makes this an interesting systems research direction: how do we bring the architecture and the software together so that programmers can get that efficiency without having to understand every detail of the hardware?

r001.rationale: It says AI algorithms keep changing and that reconfigurability supports new models and different mixes of operations.

r002.rationale: It describes mapping operations and arranging data flow, but does not propose reconfiguring only part of the system for a different computation graph.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison to static VLIW scheduling or runtime CPU scheduling.

r004.rationale: It mentions efficiency and dataflow advantages, but does not clearly state that adding dynamism must preserve the architecture’s existing advantages.
